title: Patent Wars: Who Really Invented It?
summary: Once people saw how useful the telephone was, everyone wanted a piece of it. Bell's company went to court hundreds of times against rivals, including a huge telegraph company and a Pennsylvania tinkerer who said he got there first. The courts sided with Bell, but people still argue about how much credit others, like Antonio Meucci, deserve.

sections.heading: A Telegraph Giant Changes Its Mind
paragraphs: In 1876, the most powerful communications company in the United States was Western Union. It owned telegraph lines stretching across the country, offices in thousands of towns, and close ties to inventors such as Elisha Gray and Thomas Edison. When Bell's backers offered to sell it the telephone patent, Western Union said no. (You may have seen a famous memo in which Western Union supposedly mocked the telephone as a useless toy. As Part 8 explained, that memo is almost certainly a fake. What is true is that the company turned down the chance to buy Bell's patent.)

Within about a year, Western Union's leaders realised they had made a mistake. Telephones were spreading. Businesses wanted them to talk between offices and warehouses, and doctors and shopkeepers wanted them too. If people could simply talk down a wire, they might stop sending telegrams. So Western Union decided not to buy the telephone, but to build its own.

In late 1877, Western Union and its subsidiary, the Gold and Stock Telegraph Company, set up the American Speaking Telephone Company. It had powerful weapons. It controlled telephone patents from Elisha Gray, whose caveat had been filed on the same day as Bell's patent application, and from other inventors. Most important of all, it had Edison's new carbon transmitter, which, as we saw in Part 9, made voices much louder and clearer than Bell's magnet transmitter. Western Union also had money, workers, poles and wires already strung through cities. In many places, its telephones simply sounded better than Bell's.

Imagine being one of the small team running the young Bell Telephone Company in Boston at this moment. You own the key patent, but you have little money, a handful of employees and a product that many customers now say is quieter than the competition. Your rival is one of the largest corporations in the country. It looked like a fight between a rowboat and a battleship.

Bell's side responded in two ways. First, it improved its own phones. The company acquired Emile Berliner's transmitter patent and adopted Francis Blake's carbon transmitter, so it no longer had to fear Edison's sound quality. Second, it hired a determined young manager named Theodore Vail, who became general manager in 1878. Vail would later shape the whole Bell System. One of his first jobs was to make sure the company's agents across the country stood firm and did not sell out to Western Union.

Then Bell's company took the boldest step of all: it went to court. In September 1878, it sued a man named Peter A. Dowd, who was an agent for Western Union's telephone business. Suing a single agent might seem small, but everyone understood the real target. If the court agreed that Dowd's telephones broke Bell's patent, then the whole Western Union telephone business was breaking it too.

sections.heading: The Deal of November 1879
paragraphs: The Dowd case became a giant contest of evidence. Lawyers for both sides gathered testimony about who had experimented with what, and when. Western Union's lawyers looked for any earlier inventor whose work might cancel Bell's patent. Bell's lawyers argued that Bell was the first to describe and claim the essential method: sending speech by a current that varied in the same way as the sound itself.

As the evidence piled up, Western Union's own legal team grew worried. The company's lead lawyer, George Gifford, reportedly came to believe that Bell's patent would hold up in court. At the same time, Western Union faced other troubles, including pressure from the financier Jay Gould, who was trying to gain control of the telegraph business. Fighting an expensive, possibly losing battle over telephones began to look like a bad idea.

On November 10, 1879, the two sides settled. Under the agreement, Western Union left the telephone business. It handed over its telephone network and its telephone patents, including those based on the work of Gray and Edison, to the Bell company. In return, Western Union was to receive a share of Bell's telephone rental income for years to come, usually described as about 20 percent, and the Bell company agreed to stay out of the telegraph business. Each giant, in effect, kept to its own territory.

For the Bell company, it was a stunning victory. Overnight it gained tens of thousands of telephones in cities across the country, Edison's and Gray's patents, and freedom from its most dangerous rival. Its share price soared. In early 1880, the company reorganised as the American Bell Telephone Company, and in 1881 it bought a controlling interest in Western Electric, the manufacturing company Elisha Gray had helped found, so it could build its own equipment.

The telephone fight was not only American. In Britain, Edison developed an unusual loud receiver that used a moistened chalk cylinder, and an Edison telephone company competed with a Bell company in London. Rather than fight on for years, the two British companies merged in 1880 to form the United Telephone Company. Again and again in these early years, rivals discovered that combining their patents was cheaper than battling over them.

There is a twist worth noticing. The settlement was a business deal, not a court verdict. No judge had ruled on whether Gray or anyone else had invented the telephone first. Western Union recognised Bell's patent as part of the agreement, but the deeper question of credit had not been answered. That left the door open for many more challengers.

sections.heading: Six Hundred Courtroom Battles
paragraphs: Bell's 1876 patent, number 174,465, and his second telephone patent of January 1877 were extremely valuable. Together they gave the Bell company control over the basic telephone in the United States until they ran out in the early 1890s. Anyone who wanted to make or rent telephones without paying Bell had only one real option: prove that the patents were invalid. And so, all through the 1880s, challengers lined up.

It helps to remember what a patent actually gives. In the United States at that time, a patent lasted 17 years. During that time, nobody else could make, use or sell the invention without the patent owner's permission. In exchange, the inventor had to describe the invention publicly, so that everyone could learn from it and freely use it once the patent ran out. For Bell's company, the patent was like a fence around a field: as long as the fence stood, the company could decide who was allowed in and how much they paid.

Bell's company fought an astonishing number of legal battles over its patents: around 600 in all. One careful count lists 587 court challenges, five of which reached the United States Supreme Court. Aside from a couple of minor contract disputes, the company never lost a case that ran all the way to a final judgment. Historians sometimes call this period the 'telephone patent wars'.

The challengers came in all shapes. Some were respectable scientists. Amos Dolbear, a physics professor at Tufts College near Boston, had built telephones of his own, including a receiver that worked using static electricity rather than an electromagnet. His backers argued that Bell's patent should not cover such different designs. Some were companies with grand names, like the Molecular Telephone Company. Others were small local businesses hoping that one lucky ruling would let them set up exchanges without paying Bell.

Why did Bell keep winning? The key was the way his patent was written. Besides describing particular devices, it claimed the method of sending speech and other sounds by an electric current that changes in the same pattern as the sound waves. Courts decided that this method was Bell's invention. So even if a rival used a different transmitter, a different receiver or a different material, it still used Bell's method if it carried a voice by a changing current. That made it very hard to build any working telephone without bumping into Bell's patent.

These cases were not just paperwork. Bell himself had to give long sworn statements, called depositions, answering detailed questions about his notebooks, experiments and letters. Lawyers combed through everything he had ever written. He found the process exhausting and sometimes deeply upsetting, because rival lawyers were not only disputing his work but suggesting he was dishonest. Still, his detailed records, kept carefully over years, proved to be among his strongest defences.

sections.heading: The Tinkerer from Eberly's Mill
paragraphs: Of all the challengers, the most colourful was Daniel Drawbaugh. Born on July 14, 1827, at Eberly's Mill in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, not far from Harrisburg, Drawbaugh was a bearded country mechanic who could make almost anything in his little workshop near Yellow Breeches Creek. Over his long life he patented machines for shaping barrel staves, pneumatic tools, folding boxes and a coin-sorting device. Neighbours knew him as a gifted, endlessly busy tinkerer.

Drawbaugh claimed that he had built a working telephone years before Bell, as early as about 1867, using, among other things, a teacup as part of his transmitter. He said he had been too poor to apply for a patent at the time and only sought one around 1880, after Bell's telephone had become famous. A company called the People's Telephone Company backed his claim, hoping that if Drawbaugh were recognised as the first inventor, Bell's patent would collapse and People's could run telephones freely.

The case became a spectacle. Drawbaugh's side gathered many neighbours and acquaintances who swore that, years earlier, they had heard sounds or speech through the gadgets in his workshop. Bell's side pointed out that Drawbaugh had no dated drawings, no published descriptions and no patent applications from those years, and that memories of events a decade old could easily be mistaken. Drawbaugh's own testimony did not help him: when asked how he had arrived at his invention, he answered that he did not remember how he came to it. For a man claiming one of the great inventions of the century, that sounded unconvincing to many observers.

Imagine the scene in the lower courts and finally in Washington, D.C.: stacks of printed testimony thousands of pages long, models of strange early instruments, rows of lawyers in dark suits. People's Telephone was represented by an eloquent lawyer named Lysander Hill, who argued so persuasively that some observers thought he might actually win.

Drawbaugh's case was grouped with several others, including those of Dolbear and the Molecular Telephone Company, into what became known as the Telephone Cases. The Supreme Court heard arguments in early 1887 and announced its decision on March 19, 1888. Two justices took no part, so seven judges decided. The vote was 4 to 3 in favour of Bell. Chief Justice Morrison Waite wrote for the majority that Bell's patent was valid and that he was the first inventor of the method of transmitting speech by electricity.

The three dissenting justices, led by Justice Joseph Bradley, came to the opposite view about Drawbaugh. They believed the evidence showed that Drawbaugh had made a working telephone before Bell, which would have made Bell's patent invalid. So the most famous legal decision about who invented the telephone was won by a single vote. The written decision was so long that it fills most of a whole volume of the official reports of the Supreme Court.

Drawbaugh never received the credit he wanted, but he kept inventing for the rest of his life. He died on November 2, 1911, reportedly while working in his laboratory. Today a Pennsylvania historical marker near his old workshop remembers him.

sections.heading: The Government Steps In, and Meucci's Last Chance
paragraphs: Meanwhile, another battle had begun, this time with the United States government itself as the challenger. In 1885 and 1886, a scandal broke over a rival firm called the Pan-Electric Telephone Company. It turned out that several powerful politicians held shares in it, including the US Attorney General, Augustus Garland, the government's top lawyer. When the government began moving to attack Bell's patent, critics accused officials of trying to help a company they had money in. The scandal was embarrassing, but the legal case went ahead.

On January 13, 1887, the United States government filed a lawsuit asking the courts to cancel Bell's patent on the grounds of fraud and misrepresentation. One part of the case concerned Bell's patent application of 1876 and the patent office's handling of Elisha Gray's caveat. A former patent examiner, Zenas Wilber, gave sworn statements on the matter that contradicted each other, which made his evidence hard to trust. As Part 7 explained, whether Bell saw anything improper from Gray's papers is still debated by historians and has never been proven.

The government's case also drew on the story of Antonio Meucci. As we saw in Part 5, Meucci was an Italian inventor living on Staten Island, New York, who had worked for years on a voice-carrying device he called the telettrofono. He had set up a speaking link between rooms of his home, partly so he could talk with his wife, Ester, who was disabled by severe arthritis. He filed a patent caveat on December 28, 1871, but by his own account he could not afford the $10 fee to keep it going after 1874.

Meucci's life had been hard. He had lost money in business, his house had been sold at auction in 1861, and he had been badly injured in a steamboat boiler explosion. He also said that working models he had given to a telegraph company laboratory had been lost. When a company called the Globe Telephone Company tried to use his claims to challenge Bell, the Bell company sued it. In 1887, a federal judge, William J. Wallace, ruled against Globe, deciding that what Meucci had described was a mechanical device, more like a tin-can 'string telephone' than an electric telephone. Meucci's supporters, then and now, have called that ruling unfair.

The government's lawsuit, however, was still alive. In 1888 the Supreme Court decided that the government did have the right to bring such a case, and sent it back for trial. But the case moved slowly. Antonio Meucci died in October 1889, still poor, never having seen his claims fully tested. Bell's original telephone patent expired in 1893 and his second in 1894. With the patents gone, there was little left to fight over, and the government finally dropped the case in 1897. No court ever gave a final ruling in that case on Meucci's claim to be the true inventor.

For many Italian Americans especially, Meucci became a symbol of the poor, struggling immigrant inventor who never got his chance. His home on Staten Island, where his friend the Italian hero Giuseppe Garibaldi had also lived for a time, is today the Garibaldi-Meucci Museum.

sections.heading: A Resolution in 2002
paragraphs: More than a century later, Meucci's story returned to Washington. On June 11, 2002, the United States House of Representatives passed House Resolution 269, introduced by Representative Vito Fossella of New York, whose district included Staten Island.

The resolution told Meucci's story: his work in Staten Island, his 1871 caveat, his poverty, the lost models and the government's 1887 lawsuit, which ended without a final decision after his death. It included the striking statement that if Meucci had been able to pay the $10 fee to keep his caveat alive after 1874, no patent could have been issued to Bell. It ended by declaring that the life and achievements of Antonio Meucci should be recognised and that his work in the invention of the telephone should be acknowledged.

It is important to understand what this resolution did and did not do. A House resolution like this one is an expression of opinion, sometimes called a 'sense of the House' resolution. It is not a law, it was never passed by the Senate, and it did not change any patent, court ruling or official record. It did not declare Meucci 'the' inventor of the telephone, although many newspapers at the time reported it that way.

Resolutions of this kind are quite common. Congress regularly passes non-binding statements honouring scientists, athletes, soldiers, anniversaries and communities. They can matter a great deal to the people being honoured, because they put a story into the official record and draw public attention to it. But they are not trials, and nobody cross-examines the evidence the way a court would.

The resolution also caused friction in Canada, where Bell is a national hero: he worked on the telephone at his family's home in Brantford, Ontario, and later lived in Nova Scotia. About ten days after the US vote, Canada's House of Commons passed its own motion stating that Alexander Graham Bell was the inventor of the telephone. Some historians were sharply critical of the US resolution too. Robert Bruce, a respected biographer of Bell, argued that Meucci's claim did not stand up and that Meucci had not understood the basic principles of the electric telephone. Meucci's supporters reply that the evidence was never properly judged because he was too poor to defend it.

sections.heading: So Who Really Invented the Telephone?
paragraphs: After all these lawsuits, resolutions and arguments, what is the fairest answer? It helps to separate a few different questions that often get mixed together.

Who first imagined sending speech by electricity? Charles Bourseul described the idea in France in 1854, and others dreamed of it too. Who built early devices that carried musical tones and some speech? Johann Philipp Reis in Germany, in 1861. Who worked for years on a voice-carrying device in America before Bell? Antonio Meucci, and possibly Daniel Drawbaugh, though both claims depend on evidence that was disputed in court. Who arrived at a closely similar design at almost exactly the same moment? Elisha Gray, who filed his caveat on the very day Bell's application arrived.

Who received the key patent, made it work reliably, demonstrated it to the world and turned it into a successful business? Alexander Graham Bell, with Thomas Watson building the instruments and Gardiner Hubbard and others providing money and organisation. And who made it loud and practical enough to cover real distances? Edison, Berliner, Hughes, Blake and many engineers whose names are rarely remembered.

Historians today generally agree that Bell holds the key patent and deserves major credit, but that he did not work in a vacuum. Many people were circling the same idea at the same time, because the scientific pieces, electromagnets, batteries, telegraph wires and the study of sound, were all available. When that happens, inventions often appear in several places at once. The patent system rewards whoever wins the legal race, which is not always the same as being the only person with the idea.

This pattern, sometimes called simultaneous or multiple invention, is surprisingly common in the history of science. Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz both developed calculus in the late 1600s. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the idea of evolution by natural selection independently in the 1850s. In the telephone's own story, Edison, Berliner and Hughes all arrived at carbon transmitters within months of each other. When an idea is 'in the air', the person remembered is often the one who files first, builds the best working version, or wins in court, and the others become footnotes, even though their work was real.

The patent wars also had big consequences for ordinary people. Because Bell's company controlled the basic telephone until 1893 and 1894, it could set prices and decide where to build. When the patents expired, thousands of independent telephone companies sprang up, especially in small towns and farming areas the Bell company had ignored. Competition brought prices down and spread telephones far more widely.

And that spreading created a brand-new problem. In the very first years, telephones were rented in pairs and wired directly to each other: one line from your shop to your house, for example. That works for two phones. But imagine a town with a hundred phones, each wanting to call any of the others. You would need thousands of separate wires zigzagging over every street. If everyone was going to get a telephone, someone needed a smarter way to connect them, and the answer would be a busy room full of plugs, cords and voices calling out 'Number, please.'

deepDive: Legal historians often treat the Telephone Cases, 126 U.S. 1 (1888), as a landmark in how broad a patent claim can be. Bell's fifth claim covered 'the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically' by causing electrical undulations similar in form to the vibrations of the voice. The majority led by Chief Justice Morrison Waite read this as a valid claim to a method, not merely to a specific machine, so later designs using carbon transmitters or different receivers still infringed. Critics then and now have argued this was extraordinarily wide protection for a patent whose own described liquid transmitter was not even its main embodiment. Decades earlier, in O'Reilly v. Morse, the Court had struck down Samuel Morse's broadest claim to all uses of electromagnetism for printing at a distance, so the telephone ruling is often compared with it. The 4 to 3 split is also notable: Justices Horace Gray and Lucius Lamar did not take part, and Justice Joseph Bradley's dissent, joined by Stephen Field and John Marshall Harlan, accepted Drawbaugh's evidence of priority. With two more participating justices the result could, in principle, have been different. Debates about Gray and the patent office centre on the timing of filings on February 14, 1876, on marginal notes about variable resistance in Bell's application, and on the conflicting affidavits of examiner Zenas Wilber; historians such as Robert Bruce defend Bell, while writers such as Seth Shulman and A. Edward Evenson have argued that Bell benefited improperly. None of this has been settled by new decisive evidence. Meucci's case rests partly on notebooks and witness statements; supporters, including researcher Basilio Catania, argue he understood electrical speech, while the 1887 Globe decision concluded his caveat described a mechanical device. The 2002 House Resolution 269 is non-binding, and Canada's House of Commons answered with a motion naming Bell the inventor. The economics also matter: the settlement of November 10, 1879 removed Western Union from telephony, and Bell's patent monopoly until 1893 to 1894 shaped the American telephone industry for a century.
funFact: The US Supreme Court's 1888 decision in the Telephone Cases, which upheld Bell's patent by just one vote, was so long that it takes up most of a whole volume of the official Supreme Court reports.
